newRows.name: The Anglican Communion in the Twentieth Century
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). It rests on the records of Lambeth and of the Anglican Consultative Council, and on two standard histories. Its window opens in 1906, where the Victorian Church of England entry ends.
newRows.sourcing: Rich: the records of the Lambeth Conference and of the Anglican Consultative Council. Two standard histories, by Kevin Ward (2006) and William Sachs, ed. (2017), come from university presses.
newRows.floorNote: No question. In 1920 the bishops at Lambeth named the Nicene Creed as the sufficient statement of the Christian faith.
newRows.relationsSummary: It carries on from the Victorian Church of England and the Oxford Movement. Both of those entries end in 1906. In this era Anglicans also appear inside other stories, such as the East African Revival and the Church of South India.
newRows.why: By 2006, Kevin Ward found, most Anglicans lived outside the West. Their bishops met at Lambeth. There they spoke on Christian unity, on birth control and on sexuality.

sources.work: Lambeth Conference 1920, Resolution 9, 'An Appeal to All Christian People' (15 August 1920)
sources.note: Text and date verified; the report's publisher is not confirmed.

sources.work: Committee of the Council of the English Church Union, The English Church Union and the Lambeth Conference: The Report of the Committee of the Council (London: English Church Union, 1931)
sources.note: A contemporary report giving the text of the 1930 resolution on parenthood and its recorded vote.

sources.work: Anglican Consultative Council, ACC-1 resolutions (Limuru, Kenya, 1971)
Lambeth Conference 1998, Resolution I.10, 'Human Sexuality'
sources.note: Title and conference verified; the vote figures are not confirmed.

William L. Sachs, ed., The Oxford History of Anglicanism, Volume V: Global Anglicanism, c. 1910-2000 (Oxford University Press, 2017)

newRows.longDescription: The bishops of the Anglican churches met at Lambeth in 1920, 1930, 1968 and 1998, among other years. In 1920 they sent out an Appeal to All Christian People. It named the Scriptures, the Nicene Creed, the two sacraments and a shared ministry as the ground of a future unity. In 1930 they voted 193 to 67 on limiting or avoiding parenthood. Where a couple clearly felt a moral duty to do so, they said, the method must be decided on Christian principles. In 1968 Lambeth proposed an Anglican Consultative Council. It first met at Limuru, Kenya, in 1971. Over the century most of the Communion came to live outside the West. In 1998 the bishops passed a resolution on human sexuality. In June 2008 the first Global Anglican Future Conference (GAFCON) met in Jerusalem. It issued the Jerusalem Declaration.
newRows.teaser: A worldwide family of churches whose bishops met at Lambeth, and whose members came to live mostly outside the West.
voices: The Lambeth Conference of 1920 — whose Appeal to All Christian People named the Nicene Creed as the sufficient statement of the Christian faith
The Lambeth Conference of 1930 — whose resolution on limiting parenthood was the only one that year with a recorded vote
The Anglican Consultative Council — proposed at Lambeth in 1968, and first meeting at Limuru, Kenya, in 1971
The Global Anglican Future Conference — which met in Jerusalem in June 2008 and issued the Jerusalem Declaration
newRows.legacy: By 2006, Kevin Ward found, most of its members belonged to churches outside the West. Ward and William Sachs both tell its twentieth century as one Communion's story.

livingEvidence.basis: Settled on dated evidence. Settled on a verified 2022 report of a Lambeth Conference.
livingEvidence.evidence: Vatican News, 'Fifteenth Lambeth Conference kicks off in Canterbury' (July 2022): independent news; verified.
livingEvidence.grade: CR (Contemporary-Reported); newest dated item 2022, newest verified 2022

newRows.name: The Rescue Mission Movement
newRows.region: New York, then the U.S. and Canada
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1906, when mission leaders in New York formed a federation of gospel missions. Its first missions are older, from 1872, and are told here as its beginning.
newRows.sourcing: Moderate: one study by a scholar, Norris Magnuson's Salvation in the Slums (1977). The network's own history adds to it. So do a 1972 article in Christianity Today and the Billy Graham Center Archives.
newRows.floorNote: No question. The union, later named Citygate Network, published a statement of faith. It named one God, eternally Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It said that Jesus Christ was God, born of a virgin, and that he rose bodily from the dead.
newRows.relationsSummary: The Salvation Army did the same kind of work, but as a church body. Norris Magnuson counts the rescue missions among the revival-based welfare movements of 1865 to 1920.
newRows.why: In 1872 Jerry McAuley opened a mission on Water Street in New York. Others followed. In 1906 mission leaders in New York joined in a federation. A historian counts these missions among the revival-based welfare movements of 1865 to 1920.

sources.work: Citygate Network (formerly the Association of Gospel Rescue Missions), 'Our History'
sources.note: The network's own history: the 1906 federation, the 1913 union, the 2000 association. The founding documents themselves are not seen.

sources.work: Billy Graham Center Archives, Wheaton College, 'When Did We See You a Stranger' and the 1999 'rescue talk' exhibit

sources.work: Encyclopedia of Chicago, 'Pacific Garden Mission'
'100 Years of Least, Last, and Lost', Christianity Today (10 November 1972)
sources.note: Author and exact wording not confirmed.

newRows.longDescription: In 1872 Jerry McAuley opened a mission on Water Street in New York. Others followed. In 1877 Colonel George Clarke and his wife Sarah opened the Pacific Garden Mission in Chicago, it seems with no tie to McAuley. It aimed to be 'a harbor for wrecked and ruined lives'. In 1906 mission leaders in New York formed a National Federation of Gospel Missions. On 17 September 1913 a wider body followed, the International Union of Gospel Missions, with about fifty missions. The historian Norris Magnuson counts the rescue missions among the revival-based welfare movements of 1865 to 1920. He argues that their welfare work came from their commitment to evangelism and personal holiness. By 1972 the union counted some 350 members. In 2000 it became the Association of Gospel Rescue Missions.
newRows.teaser: City gospel missions, from New York's Water Street in 1872 to a union of missions in 1913.
voices: Jerry McAuley — whose mission on Water Street, New York, opened in 1872
Colonel George Clarke and Sarah Clarke — who opened the Pacific Garden Mission in Chicago in 1877
Sidney Whittemore — who led the International Union of Gospel Missions at its founding in 1913
newRows.legacy: The union took a new name in 2000, the Association of Gospel Rescue Missions. In 2010 it was still the movement's network.

newRows.name: The Christian Homeschool Movement
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in March 1983, when the Home School Legal Defense Association was launched. The Christian day schools and a book of 1975 came before it and are told here as background. It covers only the Christian root of homeschooling that Mitchell Stevens names, not the movement as a whole.
newRows.sourcing: Moderate: two studies from university presses, by Mitchell Stevens (2001) and Alan Peshkin (1986), and a history by Milton Gaither (2008). The carriers' own texts add to them.
newRows.floorNote: No question. In 2020 its legal defense association set out what it believed. It named one God in three Persons. It said that God became a human being in Jesus Christ, the Son, who rose bodily from the dead. The statement bound the association's leaders and staff, not its members.
newRows.relationsSummary: Alan Peshkin studied a fundamentalist Baptist school. That ties this entry to Fundamentalism. Mitchell Stevens also traced a second root of homeschooling, a liberal one. It was not Christian, so it stays outside this entry.
newRows.why: Sociologist Mitchell Stevens found that homeschooling was an organized movement, not a scatter of private choices. He traced one of its two roots to the Christian day schools of the 1960s and 1970s. In 1983 a legal defense group for homeschool families followed.

newRows.longDescription: Sociologist Mitchell Stevens traced one root of homeschooling to the Christian day-school movement of the 1960s and 1970s. Alan Peshkin spent eighteen months in one such school, a Baptist school in Illinois, in the late 1970s. He called it a 'total world'. Raymond and Dorothy Moore's Better Late Than Early (1975) argued that formal lessons should wait until a child was older. Around 1982 James Dobson interviewed Raymond Moore about the book on the air. Some families who heard the broadcast began to teach their children at home. In March 1983 two homeschooling fathers, the lawyers Michael Farris and J. Michael Smith, launched the Home School Legal Defense Association with their wives. At the time, homeschooling was legal in only a handful of states. A reviewer of Stevens's study summed the movement up as 'a woman's enterprise, in which men are usually junior partners'.
newRows.teaser: In 1983 two lawyers, both fathers who taught their children at home, set up a legal defense group for homeschool families.
voices: Raymond and Dorothy Moore — whose Better Late Than Early (1975) argued that formal lessons should wait until a child was older
Michael Farris and J. Michael Smith — homeschooling fathers and lawyers who launched the Home School Legal Defense Association in March 1983
Mitchell Stevens — the sociologist whose Kingdom of Children (2001) traced homeschooling's Christian root
newRows.legacy: In 2001 Mitchell Stevens told the story of homeschooling as a social movement.

newRows.name: The Liturgical Movement
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window closes in 1962, at the Second Vatican Council, where Fenwick and Spinks close the Catholic movement. The parish after the Council has its own entry.
newRows.sourcing: Rich: its own journal from 1926 and its English handbooks of 1935 and 1937. Two academic histories, by Keith Pecklers (1998) and by John Fenwick and Bryan Spinks (1995), tell its story.
newRows.floorNote: No question. Its carriers were Benedictine houses of the Catholic Church and Anglican parishes. Both churches held to the Nicene Creed.
newRows.relationsSummary: It ran through Benedictine abbeys, journals and parishes, not through the Vatican. The entry on the Catholic Church before the Council names it once. The entry on the parish after the Council takes up what came of it.
newRows.why: Historians date the popular liturgical movement from an address at Malines, Belgium, in 1909. It reached America through Saint John's Abbey in Collegeville. There the journal Orate Fratres was founded in 1926. In England, Gabriel Hebert's books gave the Parish Communion movement its handbook.

sources.work: 'Liturgical Movement, The', An Episcopal Dictionary of the Church (online at episcopalchurch.org)
sources.note: Dates the popular liturgical movement from Beauduin's address at Malines in 1909. Print edition details not confirmed.

newRows.longDescription: In 1909 Dom Lambert Beauduin spoke at the National Congress of Catholic Action in Malines, Belgium. Historians date the popular liturgical movement from that address. In 1926 Virgil Michel of Saint John's Abbey in Minnesota founded the journal Orate Fratres, the movement's voice. He also set up the Liturgical Press. Keith Pecklers showed how closely its American leaders tied worship to social justice in the 1930s and 1940s. In England, Gabriel Hebert published Liturgy and Society in 1935. The Church Times later called it 'the Bible of the Parish Communion Movement'. Hebert's collection The Parish Communion (1937) set out a practice that changed the pattern of Sunday-morning worship.
newRows.teaser: A movement to renew worship began with a talk in Malines in 1909. It spread to Catholic abbeys and Anglican parishes.
voices: Dom Lambert Beauduin — whose address at Malines in 1909 historians take as the movement's start
Virgil Michel — who founded the journal Orate Fratres at Saint John's Abbey in 1926
Gabriel Hebert — whose Liturgy and Society (1935) was called 'the Bible of the Parish Communion Movement'
newRows.legacy: John Fenwick and Bryan Spinks tell its story across many churches: Catholic, Anglican, Eastern and North American. They close the Catholic part in 1962.

livingEvidence.basis: A closed tradition. Its history closes at the Council, and the entry on the parish after 1962 carries what followed.
livingEvidence.evidence: Societas Liturgica, Newsletter 51 (Autumn 2025): a society for liturgical study and renewal, alive today; own voice; verified. It is not counted as the movement itself.
livingEvidence.grade: n/a (flag false on a documented end)

newRows.name: The Third Wave & the Vineyard
newRows.informalName: The Vineyard and the Third Wave
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1982, when the Signs and Wonders course began at Fuller Seminary. The entry on the charismatic renewal and the Jesus movement ends where the Vineyard began, in 1982.
newRows.sourcing: Rich: Fuller Seminary's archive of the course and its founders' books. Fuller's own study of the course and the work of four scholars add to them.
newRows.floorNote: No question. The Vineyard churches' statement of faith named one God in three persons of one substance. It called Christ fully God and fully human in one person, raised from the dead on the third day. Copies of it published by others date its adoption by the association's board to November 1994.
newRows.relationsSummary: It follows the charismatic renewal and the Jesus movement. That entry names the Vineyard of 1982 as the start of the third wave. The Toronto Blessing of 1994 grew inside one of its churches.
newRows.why: In 1982 John Wimber began teaching 'Signs and Wonders' at Fuller Seminary. C. Peter Wagner called the stream 'the Third Wave'. Its people sought the gifts of the Spirit. But they did not take on Pentecostal or charismatic theology or worship styles.

newRows.longDescription: In 1982 John Wimber and C. Peter Wagner began teaching MC510, 'Signs and Wonders', at Fuller Theological Seminary in Pasadena. The course ran until 1985 and drew controversy. Fuller's faculty dropped it in early 1986 and published its own study, Ministry and the Miraculous, in 1987. Wagner called the stream 'the Third Wave'. Its people believed in the power and gifts of the Holy Spirit. Yet they did not adopt Pentecostal or charismatic theology or worship styles. Wimber set out his method in Power Evangelism in 1985. In 1994 a revival called the Toronto Blessing began at the Toronto Airport Vineyard. The Vineyard association cut its ties with that church in December 1995. Margaret Poloma published a study of the revival in 1997. Jon Bialecki later studied 'the Third Wave' by name, and the Vineyard as 'an American charismatic movement'.
newRows.teaser: It began with a seminary course called 'Signs and Wonders'. Its churches sought the gifts of the Spirit without becoming Pentecostal.
voices: John Wimber — who taught the Signs and Wonders course at Fuller and wrote Power Evangelism (1985)
C. Peter Wagner — who taught the course with Wimber and coined the name 'Third Wave'
Ministry and the Miraculous (1987) — Fuller Seminary's own study of the course it had dropped
newRows.legacy: In 1997 Donald Miller studied the Vineyard beside two other new church networks. Jon Bialecki's study of its churches followed in 2017.

newRows.name: Promise Keepers & the Christian Men's Movement
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1990, when Promise Keepers began. The size of its 1997 rally in Washington rests on a crowd estimate.
newRows.sourcing: Moderate. A study by John Bartkowski (2004) comes from a university press. An encyclopedia entry, the movement's own book of 1994 and news reports of the time add to it.
newRows.floorNote: No question, on a reported text. In 1997 a newspaper reported its statement of faith. It named one God in three persons, the deity of Jesus, and salvation through his death.
newRows.relationsSummary: Its setting was evangelical, like that of the megachurches and of Lausanne-era evangelicals. But its focus on men was its own. James Mathisen set it apart from the wider men's movement.
newRows.why: In 1990 a college football coach and a friend started a ministry for men. Its first members called themselves Promise Keepers. By 1996 its rallies had filled 22 stadiums with nearly 1.2 million men. Each man made seven promises. Among them, he would keep close friendships with other men, stay pure and keep his marriage strong. He would also reach across lines of race and church.

newRows.longDescription: On 20 March 1990, Bill McCartney, the University of Colorado football coach, drove with a friend to Pueblo. From that trip grew a group of about seventy men who called themselves Promise Keepers. In 1991, 4,200 men met at the university's basketball arena. In 1996, 22 stadium rallies drew nearly 1.2 million men. Each man made seven promises, published in 1994 as Seven Promises of a Promise Keeper. They pledged purity, strong marriages, and friendship across racial and denominational barriers. On 4 October 1997 a crowd estimated at about a million men gathered in Washington, D.C., for Stand in the Gap. In March 1998 the ministry began laying off 345 paid staff. Sociologist John Bartkowski later traced the rise and fall of this Christian men's movement.
newRows.teaser: In 1990 a football coach had an idea. It filled stadiums with men who made seven promises, and in 1997 it reached Washington.
voices: Bill McCartney and Dave Wardell — who founded Promise Keepers in 1990

newRows.legacy: In 2001 James Mathisen called it 'the decade's most unexpected and immediately successful movement within the American church'.

At the 1974 congress, Ralph and Roberta Winter prepared a paper on the peoples that existing missions did not reach. In 1997 the Southern Baptist International Mission Board took up an approach called the Church Planting Movement. David Garrison set it out in a book in 2004. Evangelical relief agencies worked on the same ground, and some were older than the congress. Tearfund grew out of the Evangelical Alliance in 1968. Brian Stanley's history names this evangelical age after Billy Graham and John Stott. Graham's evangelistic association was incorporated in 1950.

registerEdits.old: Four separately founded bodies are carried together here for the map's economy, not because they share a confession — they do not, and each is described from its own published texts. Iglesia ni Cristo was registered in the Philippines on 27 July 1914; its own history presents Felix Manalo as God's messenger for the last days, and its magazine Pasugo has published its teaching since February 1939. The Way International began as Victor Paul Wierwille's Vesper Chimes radio ministry in 1942 and took its later name in 1955; his Power for Abundant Living appeared in 1971 and Jesus Christ Is Not God in 1975, a title that states its own position. The Unification Church, later known as the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification, was founded in Seoul on 1 May 1954 by Sun Myung Moon, whose Divine Principle appeared in Korean in 1966. La Luz del Mundo was founded in Guadalajara on 6 April 1926 by Eusebio Joaquín González, and from 1964 was led by a second apostle in succession from him.
registerEdits.new: Three separately founded bodies share this entry, but not a confession. Each is described from its own published texts. The Way International began in 1942 as Victor Paul Wierwille's Vesper Chimes radio ministry. It took its later name in 1955. His Power for Abundant Living appeared in 1971, and Jesus Christ Is Not God in 1975, a title that states its own position. Sun Myung Moon founded the Unification Church in Seoul on 1 May 1954. It was later known as the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification. Moon's Divine Principle appeared in Korean in 1966. Eusebio Joaquín González founded La Luz del Mundo in Guadalajara on 6 April 1926. From 1964 a second apostle led it, in succession from him.

registerEdits.old: All four were still active in 2010. Iglesia ni Cristo had passed through two successions, in 1963 and 2009. La Luz del Mundo had passed through one, in 1964, and The Way through two changes of leadership after its founder. The Unification Church was still led by its founder. Iglesia ni Cristo's own counts ran to millions, and it was the largest church founded in the Philippines. No independent count is cited here. Court records are part of these bodies' public record too. The Way's leadership changes ran alongside litigation, and in 1982 a federal jury convicted Sun Myung Moon of filing false tax returns. Those are matters of public record and part of any honest telling.

Its magazine Pasugo carried its teaching from February 1939. In 2010, by its own counts, it was the largest church founded in the Philippines. No independent count is cited here.
registerEdits.new: Iglesia ni Cristo, 'the Church of Christ', was registered with the government of the Philippines on 27 July 1914. It was registered under Felix Y. Manalo, and its own history presented him as God's messenger for the last days. It honored Jesus as Lord and Savior but taught that he was not God. From February 1939 its magazine Pasugo, in Tagalog and English, set out its teaching. It passed through two changes of leader, in 1963 and 2009. By its own counts it was, by 2010, the largest church founded in the Philippines. No independent count is cited here, and independent scholarship on the church is thin.
